title: Targeted sequencing enhances detection of pangolin trafficking hotspots and dynamics of both domestic and global trade markets
experiments_summary: The study developed and applied a hybridization-based targeted sequencing (gene-capture) approach for all eight pangolin species, focusing on three heavily trafficked species: white-bellied pangolin (Phataginus tricuspis), Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica), and Chinese pangolin (M. pentadactyla). A custom myBaits v5 kit of 671 loci (~607–627 kbp) was designed using a dual-reference bait strategy (one African, one Asian reference species), incorporating loci selected for relative evolutionary rates (n=414) and biological relevance (n=257), with 40K probes at 3× tiling and 70mer baits. The kit was validated both in silico (read-mapping to baits) and in vitro (capture) across all eight species. A total of 711 samples were gene-captured from 15 museum collections (n=122) and tissue collections (n=589). An additional 92 whole-genome sequenced samples from prior studies were integrated, yielding 803 total samples. Samples were categorized by site-type: field sites, restricted-range markets, long-range markets, international seizures, and unknown localities. DNA extraction used NucleoSpin Tissue Mini Kit or DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit for tissue samples; museum skins were extracted via a CTAB-chloroform-isoamyl alcohol protocol, and museum bones were powdered in liquid nitrogen and extracted with an EDTA-based buffer. Libraries were prepared using Illumina TruSeq Nano HT kit with unique dual indexes; fragment sizing, PCR enrichment cycles, and pooling (4–17 samples per pool) were adjusted for degradation levels. Gene capture was performed at 65°C hybridization/washing temperature. Post-capture enrichment used KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix. Paired-end sequencing was conducted on Illumina MiSeq Nano/MiSeq 2 (150/250 bp). Bioinformatic processing used the nf-core EAGER v2.4.5 pipeline: quality control with FastQC and fastp/AdapterRemoval, mapping with BWA-MEM (MAPQ >30), PCR duplicate removal with Picard MarkDuplicates, and mapDamage2 rescaling for museum samples. Genotyping was performed with BCFtools mpileup/call/norm, followed by VCFtools filtering (removal of indels, low-depth sites, high-missingness, low-quality variants, minor allele count <3) and linkage disequilibrium pruning with PLINK v2.0 (50-SNP window, r²>0.2). Variants under selection were identified using Tajima's D. SNP datasets were split into neutral-only and full (neutral + non-neutral) partitions. Population structure was analyzed via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using PLINK v2.0 and ADMIXTURE v1.3 (K=1–10, 10 replicates with 10-fold cross-validation, best K by Evanno method via CLUMPAK). Isolation-by-distance was assessed with Mantel tests (1,000 permutations) in adegenet, and admixture versus IBD was evaluated with triangle-plot analyses using triangulaR v0.0.1 on highly differentiated SNPs (allele frequency difference ≥0.9). Individual-level geographic assignment was performed using Locator, a deep-learning framework trained on geo-referenced field site and restricted-range market samples (P. tricuspis: 171 training/304 predicted; M. javanica: 22/129; M. pentadactyla: 16/27), run with 100 bootstrap replicates, dropout regularization (0.25), and early stopping. Assignment accuracy was assessed using three metrics: prediction variability (dispersion of 100 bootstrapped predictions), one-third hold-out predictive error (withholding ~one-third of reference samples simultaneously), and Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (iteratively withholding each reference sample). Trade distances between predicted source centroids and market/seizure locations were calculated using the Haversine formula.
